passages.title: The oath, the secret, and the two wives
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat lift the curtain on the Prophet's ﷺ own household. Something lawful and sweet — honey — was made off-limits by an oath he swore to soothe his wives; a confidence he asked to be kept was passed on; and Allah Himself steps in, first to release His Messenger from the oath, then to address the two wives involved.

One movement holds the passage together: **Allah undoing a self-imposed restriction (ayat 1–2), exposing a hidden conversation (ayah 3), and defending His Prophet ﷺ while calling the two wives back to Him (ayat 4–5).**

## The honey, and the plot behind it

Both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān open with the occasion of revelation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it as the Prophet's ﷺ daily practice to visit each of his wives after the ʿAsr prayer, inquiring about their welfare. On one such round he stayed longer than usual in one house, because honey had been offered to him there — and, as ʿĀʾishah says in Al-Bukhari's Book of Divorce, "Allah's Messenger ﷺ liked sweets and honey."

Al-Bukhari records the incident in two places, with slightly different casts:

- **In the Book of Vows**, from ʿUbayd bin ʿUmayr from ʿĀʾishah: the Prophet ﷺ used to stay a while in the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh and drink honey there. ʿĀʾishah and Ḥafṣah agreed that whichever of them he entered upon would say, *"I smell Maghāfir on you. Have you eaten Maghāfir?"* He answered: *"No, but I drank honey in the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, and I will never drink it again."* Muslim collected this same ḥadīth from ʿĀʾishah in the Book of Divorce in his Ṣaḥīḥ, with the same wording.
- **In the Book of Divorce**, from ʿĀʾishah: it was Ḥafṣah, the daughter of ʿUmar, whom a woman of her family had sent a small vessel of honey as a gift, and she gave the Prophet ﷺ a drink made from it. ʿĀʾishah, jealous, enlisted Sawdah bint Zamʿah and Ṣafiyyah: ask whether he ate Maghāfir; when he says no, ask about the odour; when he names Ḥafṣah's honey, say the honeybees might have eaten from ʿUrfuṭ. Sawdah later admitted, *"It was under compulsion that I had decided to state that which you told me."*

**What is Maghāfir?** Al-Bukhari explains that al-Maghāfir is a type of sap; Al-Jawharī says the ʿUrfuṭ is a tree of the shrub variety which secretes it. Muslim's narration: ʿĀʾishah said the Prophet ﷺ *"used to hate to have a bad odor coming from him."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a note from Muhammad Taqi Usmani that their words were spoken in an interrogative accent — framed as a *question*, not an assertion — and so were not a false statement.

The plan worked: when Ḥafṣah next offered him the drink he said, *"I do not need it."* Sawdah said, *"By Allah! We have prevented him from drinking honey"* — and ʿĀʾishah told her to keep quiet.

**Two incidents or one?** Ibn Kathir says some might say these were two separate incidents, but it is not likely the ayat were revealed about both — and he closes twice over with *"Allah knows best."* A ḥadīth Imam Ahmad collected in the Musnad names ʿĀʾishah and Ḥafṣah as the two plotters. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that some reports place the honey at Ḥafṣah's house with ʿĀʾishah, Sawdah and Ṣafiyyah as the planners; quoting Bayān-ul-Qurʼān, it allows that many incidents of a similar nature may have taken place and these verses were revealed after them.

## Ayah 1: a question, not a rebuke

*"O Prophet! Why do you forbid that which Allah has allowed to you, seeking to please your wives? And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to the opening word: the Qur'an does not address him by his name but by his prophetic title — **"O Prophet"** — which is his special honour. The correction comes wrapped in his rank.

Ibn Kathir says Allah censures His Prophet ﷺ for prohibiting himself from what Allah has allowed for him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the tone as a loving question posed by way of compassion — but notices it could still have created the misunderstanding that a major error had been committed. That is what the closing phrase is for: **"And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful."** Even supposing it had been a sin — Allah is Most-Forgiving, Very Merciful.

*Tabtaghī marḍāta azwājik* — "seeking the pleasure of your wives." Allah names the motive, and it is a tender one. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's judgement is that banning a lawful thing on oneself is permissible, and not a sin, when it is done for a genuine need or expedience (*maṣlaḥah*) — but the incident does not show that there was any such need here. He had done it for the pleasure of his wives, and in those circumstances it was not necessary for him to have pleased them.

## The ruling: forbidding yourself what Allah permitted

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out three ways one can prohibit a lawful thing for oneself, referring back to its treatment of *"O you who believe, do not make unlawful the good things that Allah has made lawful for you"* (5:87):

1. **Holding a lawful thing to be unlawful as part of one's religious belief** — this is *kufr* (disbelief) and an enormous sin.
2. **Not believing it unlawful in religion, but banning it on oneself by swearing an oath with no need to do so** — a sinful act; one must break the oath and expiate. If done for some need or advantage, it is permissible but undesirable.
3. **Neither believing it unlawful nor swearing, but resolving in the mind to abandon the lawful thing for ever** — if that resolution is made with the intention of reward, it is an innovation (*bidʿah*) in the established religion and monasticism, a reproachable sin. If it is not for reward but for some other reason — treating a physical ailment or a spiritual malady — it is absolutely permissible. Reports about some noble Sufis who abandoned certain lawful things fall under this last category.

## Ayah 2: Allah has already built the way out

*"Allah has already ordained for you the absolution from your oaths. And Allah is your Protector and He is the All-Knower, the All-Wise."*

*Taḥillat aymānikum* is the releasing, the "un-binding," of your oaths. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it simply: where it is necessary or better to break an oath, Allah has prescribed a way to absolve oneself from the liability of the oath by expiation, the details of which are given in other verses. The Prophet ﷺ did break this oath and expiate for it: as reported in Ad-Durr-ul-Manthūr, he emancipated a slave in payment of his expiation.

The ayah then names Allah **your Protector — *mawlākum***. Hold on to that word: it returns in ayah 4.

## Ayah 3: the secret, and the part he left unsaid

*"And when the Prophet disclosed a matter in confidence to one of his wives, then she told it. And Allah made it known to him; he informed part thereof and left a part. Then when he told her, she said: 'Who told you this?' He said: 'The All-Knower, the All-Aware has told me.'"*

Ibn Kathir identifies the confided matter as his words *"But I have drunk honey"* — and, on the authority of Ibrāhīm bin Mūsā from Hishām, that it also meant his words: *"I will not drink it anymore, I have taken an oath to that. Therefore, do not inform anybody about it."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that according to most versions of the authentic report the "secret" is the ban he imposed on himself regarding honey, and explains *why* he asked for secrecy: he did not want Zaynab's feelings to be hurt.

**"He informed part thereof and left a part."** When the wife divulged the secret and Allah disclosed the fact to him, he complained to her about the disclosure — but did not convey the whole of what he had learned. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads this as the Prophet's ﷺ magnanimity and high morals: had he disclosed the entire information he had received from Allah, it would have embarrassed her most profoundly.

**Who were they?** The Qur'an does not name them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that according to the best-received narratives it appears to have been Ḥafṣah whom he ﷺ directed to keep the matter secret, and she divulged it to ʿĀʾishah — as recorded in Bukhari on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās. It also transmits, from Mazharī, that some narratives report he ﷺ decided to divorce Ḥafṣah when she divulged the secret, and Allah sent Jibrīl to prevent him, on the ground that she offered many prayers and kept fasts abundantly — and that her name appears in the list of his wives in Paradise.

Notice how the ayah ends: *"The All-Knower, the All-Aware has told me."* The source is named by two of Allah's names — **al-ʿAlīm**, the All-Knower, and **al-Khabīr**, the All-Aware. Ayah 2 had already closed on *al-ʿAlīm al-Ḥakīm*: Allah knows, and He is wise.

## Ayah 4: two hearts, and who stands behind him

*"If you two turn in repentance to Allah, your hearts are indeed so inclined; but if you help one another against him, then verily, Allah is his Protector, and Jibrīl, and the righteous among the believers; and after that the angels are his helpers."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases the opening as: *if both of you repent to Allah — for your conduct calls for it — because your hearts have deviated.* What they did stemmed from their love for the Prophet ﷺ; but in consultation with one another they adopted a way that hurt him, and that is a sin for which repentance was necessary.

*Taẓāhara* is to back one another up, to form a bloc. If the two of them line up *against* him — then look who is lined up *behind* him: **Allah is his mawlā**, his Protector (the same word used in ayah 2), **and Jibrīl, and the righteous among the believers**, and after all that **the angels are ẓahīr** — his helpers. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the conclusion plainly: they will not cause him any loss; it will be the wives themselves who suffer loss.

**Who are "the righteous among the believers"?** Ibn Kathir says the phrase refers to Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and names Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān, Ad-Daḥḥāk and others as saying similarly. Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī added ʿUthmān to them; Layth bin Abī Sulaym said from Mujāhid that ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭālib is included as well. The sources give these as reported views, not as one settled answer.

## ʿUmar's account: the upper room, and the month apart

The longest narration Ibn Kathir brings is ʿUmar's own telling of the affair, recorded by Imam Ahmad from Ibn ʿAbbās — a ḥadīth that Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasāʾī also collected using various chains. In it Ibn ʿAbbās says he was eager to ask ʿUmar about the two ladies among the wives of the Prophet ﷺ referred to in ayah 4.

In the Imam Ahmad narration, Ibn ʿAbbās performed Hajj with ʿUmar, and on the way back, while pouring water over his hands for wuḍūʾ, he asked. *"I am astonished at your question, O Ibn ʿAbbās"* — the subnarrator Az-Zuhrī notes that ʿUmar did not like the question, but he still answered it: they were ʿĀʾishah and Ḥafṣah.

Then ʿUmar related the story. Quraysh used to have authority over their women; but among the Anṣār they found the women had the upper hand over their men, and Quraysh's women began acquiring the habit. When his own wife answered him back, she said: *by Allah, the wives of the Prophet ﷺ talk back to him, and some of them may not speak with him the whole day, until nightfall.* He went to his daughter Ḥafṣah, warned her not to be tempted to imitate her neighbour, "for she is more beautiful than you, and more beloved to Allah's Messenger than you" — meaning ʿĀʾishah.

Then his Anṣārī neighbour knocked at his door with grave news. ʿUmar's first thought was that the Ghassān had come to invade. Worse, the man said — Allah's Messenger ﷺ had divorced all his wives. ʿUmar prayed Ṣubḥ, went to Ḥafṣah and found her weeping; she did not know. The Prophet ﷺ was alone in an upper room. ʿUmar sought permission through a servant boy and was met with silence; he went out to the minbar and sat among people, some of whom were weeping; twice more he sent the boy in, and at last was called back and let in.

He saw the Prophet ﷺ lying on a mat with no bedding on it, the mat having left its mark on his body, and nothing of importance in the room except three hides. ʿUmar asked, *"Have you divorced your wives, O Allah's Messenger?"* He raised his eyes and replied no. ʿUmar told him the story of his own wife — and the Prophet ﷺ smiled; he told him what he had said to Ḥafṣah — and he smiled again. Then ʿUmar said: invoke Allah to make your followers prosperous, for the Persians and the Byzantines have been made prosperous and given worldly luxuries even though they do not worship Allah. The Prophet ﷺ sat upright: *"O Ibn Al-Khaṭṭāb! Do you have any doubt? These people have been given rewards of their good deeds in this world only."*

In the narration Muslim recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar had said: *"O Messenger of Allah, what trouble do you feel from your wives? If you have divorced them, verily Allah is with you, His angels, Jibrīl, Mīkāl, I, Abū Bakr and the rest of believers are with you."* ʿUmar adds that he often hoped Allah would testify to the words he uttered — and then the ayah of option was revealed, in terms close to his own. Ibn Kathir mentions other statements of ʿUmar confirmed by the Qur'an: the revelation about ḥijāb (33:53), the captive idolaters after Badr (8:67), and his suggestion to take the Station of Ibrāhīm as a place of prayer (2:125).

ʿUmar then stood at the door of the masjid and called out that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had **not** divorced his wives — and it was on that occasion, he said, that Allah revealed the ayah about people who broadcast news of security or alarm instead of referring it to the Messenger and those entrusted with authority (4:83). The same narration in Muslim notes that this occurred before ḥijāb was commanded. And in the Imam Ahmad account ʿUmar concludes: the Prophet ﷺ had sworn that he would not go to his wives for one month, because of his severe anger towards them, until Allah censured him — which is where ayah 1 comes in.

## Ayah 5: "Maybe his Lord…"

*"Maybe his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him instead of you wives better than you — submitting (muslimāt), believers (muʾmināt), obedient (qānitāt), turning to Allah in repentance (tāʾibāt), worshipping Allah sincerely (ʿābidāt), sāʾiḥāt, previously married (thayyibāt), and virgins (abkār)."*

Al-Bukhari records from Anas that ʿUmar said the wives of the Prophet ﷺ were all jealous for his affection, and that he said to them precisely this — and thereafter the ayah was revealed. Ibn Abī Ḥātim records from Anas that ʿUmar, having heard that the Mothers of the Believers had had a dispute with the Prophet ﷺ, went to advise them: either stop bothering Allah's Messenger, or Allah might provide him better wives than you. When he reached the last of them, she answered: *"O ʿUmar! Is it that the Messenger of Allah cannot advise his wives, so that you interfere between him and them?"* ʿUmar stopped upon hearing this — and Allah revealed this ayah. Ibn Kathir identifies her, as confirmed in Ṣaḥīḥ Al-Bukhari, as Umm Salamah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what the ayah answers: the possible thought that, were he to divorce them, he would probably not find women better than themselves. The reply is that nothing is beyond Allah's power — with a qualification: this does not necessarily imply that better wives than these existed at that time. Possibly they were not available then; but had the need arisen, Allah could bring such women into being.

The ayah does not say "his Lord *will*"; it says **ʿasā** — "maybe," "it is hoped that" — and it is conditional: *if* he divorces you.

Of the qualities listed, Ibn Kathir says the first five are clear in their implications. **Sāʾiḥāt** means *fasting*, and he cites a long roll of authorities — Abū Hurayrah, ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, Muhammad bin Kaʿb Al-Quraẓī, Abū ʿAbdur-Raḥmān As-Sulamī, Abū Mālik, Ibrāhīm An-Nakhaʿī, Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Ad-Daḥḥāk, Ar-Rabīʿ bin Anas, As-Suddī, and others. The last pair — previously married women and virgins — sets both in the same list of the best.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ends by observing that these verses dealt specifically with the wives of the Prophet ﷺ — their deeds, their moral reform, their discipline and training — and that similar injunctions follow for the general body of Muslims and believers. The passage leaves a household with a few things to carry:

- **Do not manufacture prohibitions.** Renouncing permanently what Allah has permitted, *with the intention of reward*, is the innovation and monasticism the sources warn against.
- **An oath binds, but is not a trap.** Ayah 2 exists so that someone who has sworn wrongly has a lawful way back — expiation, not despair.
- **Love is not a licence for the method.** What the two wives did stemmed from love for the Prophet ﷺ; still, the way they chose hurt him and called for repentance.
- **Keep back part of what you know.** Ayah 3's *"he informed part thereof and left a part"* is an ethic of confrontation in six words.
- **Check before you repeat.** People were weeping by the minbar over news nobody had verified — and ʿUmar's own comment on 4:83 was that it was he who properly investigated the matter.
- **Measure your life against three hides.** The man Allah defended with Jibrīl and the angels had nothing of importance in his room, and was content.

passages.title: The Fire, the light, and the struggle
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move the sūrah out of one household and into every household. Ayah 6 hands each believer a duty of protection — over himself and over the people in his care — and then shows him exactly what he is protecting them from. Ayah 7 shows the moment when excuses are refused. Ayah 8 opens the one door still open now, sincere repentance, and lets us see where it leads: a Day of no disgrace, and a light running ahead of the believers. Ayah 9 turns to the Prophet ﷺ with the outward face of the same struggle. Fire, light, and struggle — the passage runs from what we must flee, to what we are heading towards, to what it costs.

## "Protect yourselves and your families" (ayah 6)

The command is *qū* — protect, save. Notice the order. First *anfusakum*, "yourselves"; then *wa ahlīkum*, "and your families". A man cannot shield others from behind a fire he is standing in himself.

The early authorities read the command as practical work, not sentiment. Ibn ʿAbbās, in the report of ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, said: "Work in the obedience of Allah, avoid disobedience of Allah and order your families to remember Allah, then Allah will save you from the Fire." Mujāhid put it in one line: "Have Taqwā of Allah and order your family to have Taqwā of Him." Qatādah filled in what that looks like day to day — he obeys Allah, does not disobey Him, orders his family to obey His orders **and helps them to act upon them**, and when he sees disobedience he stops it and forbids it. Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil made it an obligation: "It is an obligation for the Muslim to teach his near family members, and his male and female slaves what Allah has made obligatory for them and what Allah has forbidden for them."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *ahlīkum*, "your families", comprehends wife, children, and slaves — male as well as female — and adds that it is not inconceivable to include full-time servants in the command as slaves are included.

**ʿUmar's question.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relays (from Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī) that when this verse came down, Sayyidunā ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) asked: "O Messenger of Allah, we understand how to save ourselves from Hell, that is, we guard ourselves against sins and carry out the Divine injunctions, but how do we safeguard our families from Hell?" The Prophet ﷺ answered: "Instruct them to refrain from deeds that Allah has prohibited, and ask them to carry out deeds that Allah has enjoined. This will rescue them from the Hell-Fire."

That answer is worth sitting with. ʿUmar knew how the verse applied to himself; what he did not know was how it reached the people in his house. He was told it reaches them through instruction — steady, unglamorous, at home.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathīr brings a hadith he says confirms the meaning of the ayah: Ahmad, Abū Dāwūd and At-Tirmidhī recorded from Ar-Rabīʿ bin Sabrah, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Order the children to pray when they reach the age of seven and when they reach the age of ten, discipline them for (not performing) it." Ibn Kathīr notes this is Abū Dāwūd's wording, and that At-Tirmidhī said the hadith is *ḥasan* (sound). The verse says *protect*; the Sunnah shows it beginning with a seven-year-old and a prayer.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a hadith — quoted there without naming a collection, so it is offered here as a teaching rather than an attributed narration — that Allah shows mercy to a person who says to his household: "O my wife and children, (be mindful of) your prayers, your fasting, your alms, your indigent, your orphan, your neighbour," with the hope that Allah will gather them all with him in Paradise. Maʿārif explains the two halves: "your prayers, your fasting" implies *take care of them, do not ignore them*; "your indigent, your orphan" implies *fulfil their rights towards them willingly and readily*. Righteous elders, it reports, said that the person deepest in punishment on the Day of Judgment will be the one whose family is ignorant and unaware of the religion.

The jurists, Maʿārif notes, pointed out from this very ayah that educating wife and children in matters of Sharīʿah obligation, and in what is lawful and unlawful, and training them diligently to act upon it, is the responsibility of every Muslim — not an optional extra for the pious.

## What you are protecting them from

Allah does not leave the Fire abstract. **"Whose fuel is men and stones."** Ibn Kathīr: the Children of Ādam will themselves be the fuel that feeds it. The *stones* he takes as the idols that were worshipped, citing Allah's words elsewhere, "Certainly you and that which you are worshipping now besides Allah, are (but) fuel for Hell!" (21:98). Everything a person put in Allah's place burns beside him. ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd, Mujāhid, Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir and As-Suddī said these are sulphur stones — more putrid, according to Mujāhid, than rotten corpses.

**"Over which are angels stern and severe."** Ibn Kathīr distinguishes the two words. *Ghilāẓ* (stern) describes their nature of behaviour: the mercy has been taken out of their hearts for those who disbelieve in Allah. *Shidād* (severe) describes their structure: powerful, strong, frightening. And then their obedience — "who disobey not the commands they receive from Allah, but do that which they are commanded" — meaning, says Ibn Kathīr, that whatever Allah commands them they rush to obey Him, without delay for even a twinkling of an eye, and they are able to fulfil the command. They are called *az-Zabāniyah*: the keepers and guards of Hell. Ibn Kathīr breaks off with a prayer — may Allah give us shelter from them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the terrifying practical point: these are guards from whom no inmate of Hell will be able to rescue himself by force, power, strength, flattery or bribery. Every escape route a human being relies on in this world — muscle, influence, charm, money — is listed and cancelled.

Note the shape of ayah 6: a command that presumes the Fire can be escaped, followed by a description that makes escaping it the only sane priority.

## Ayah 7: the door of excuses

"O you who disbelieve! Make no excuses this Day! You are being requited only for what you used to do."

Ibn Kathīr explains this as words said on the Day of Resurrection: the disbeliever will be told, "Do not offer any excuse this Day, because it will not be accepted from you; you will only be recompensed for what you used to do. Today, you will receive the punishment for your actions." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the turn of address: after advising the general body of believers in ayah 6, the address turns to those who disbelieved, who are asked not to try to make excuses, because they will not be accepted — they are merely being repaid for what they did.

The whole weight of the ayah falls on one word: *today*. There is a Day on which nothing can be said, and it is not this one. Which is precisely why the very next ayah is addressed to us, now.

## Ayah 8: repentance that is *naṣūḥ*

"O you who believe! Turn to Allah with sincere repentance."

Ibn Kathīr defines it as a true, firm repentance that erases the evil sins that preceded it, mends the shortcoming of the repenting person, and encourages and directs him to quit the evil that he used to do. So it works in three directions at once — backwards on the past, inwards on the self, forwards on behaviour.

**The language.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the two key words. *Taubah* literally means *to turn* or *to return* — in the sense of turning or withdrawing from sins. In the terminology of the Qurʼān and Sunnah it signifies regretting sins committed in the past and firmly resolving to abstain from them in future.

*Naṣūḥ* is the harder word, and Maʿārif gives two derivations:

- If taken as the infinitive of *naṣaḥa / naṣīḥah*, it signifies **to make pure and sincere** — so *taubatan naṣūḥā* is repentance free from pretence and hypocrisy, where the sinner regrets his sins and gives them up purely for the pleasure of Allah and for fear of Divine chastisement.
- If derived from *naṣāḥah*, it signifies **to repair clothes by sewing** — so the sinner is required to repair the torn clothes of his righteous deeds.

Hold both images together and you have the whole of repentance: honest motive, and patient repair work. Sin tore something; you sit down and sew.

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said *taubatan naṣūḥā* means a person should regret his past evil actions and make a firm resolve never to repeat them. Al-Kalbī described it across the three faculties: **pray for pardon with the tongue, regret in the heart, and prevent the limbs of the body from committing sins in future.**

**ʿAlī's six elements.** Sayyidunā ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked what *taubah* is, and answered that it consists of six elements (Maʿārif, from Mazharī): (1) to regret one's past evil deeds; (2) to carry out Divine duties that were missed; (3) to restore the rights that were usurped; (4) to ask forgiveness of a person who has been wronged by him physically or verbally; (5) to make a firm resolve of avoiding the sin in future; (6) to consume oneself in obedience of Allah as one thus far consumed oneself in His disobedience.

Maʿārif notes that all of these conditions are recognised by all the scholars — some have described them concisely, others in detail. Look at items (2), (3) and (4): repentance in Islam is not only a feeling in the chest. Missed obligations are made up, usurped rights go back to their owners, and wronged people are approached in person.

**"It may be that your Lord will expiate…"** The verb is *ʿasā*, "it is hoped". Ibn Kathīr is direct: when Allah says "it may be", it means He shall. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees that in this context it purports to mean a promise, and explains why the language of hope is used anyway: repentance and other righteous deeds are not the just and equal price for Paradise or for divine forgiveness. One compensation for a person's good deeds has already been given to him in this world in the form of worldly blessings; so by the law of equality it is not necessary that he be further compensated with the Garden. It depends entirely on Divine grace and favour. Maʿārif cites, from Mazharī, a hadith of Bukhārī and Muslim: "Your actions alone cannot salvage you." The Companions inquired, "O Messenger of Allah, not even you?" He replied: "No, not even me unless the Divine grace and mercy covers me."

So the ayah keeps hope and humility in the same sentence. It is a promise, phrased so that no one thinks he has earned it.

## The Day of no disgrace, and the light

"…the Day that Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believe with him."

Ibn Kathīr: on the Day of Resurrection Allah will not disgrace those who believed in the Prophet ﷺ. Then, "Their light will run forward before them and in their right hands" — Ibn Kathīr refers the reader to his explanation in Sūrat al-Ḥadīd.

And in the middle of that scene, the believers are still making duʿāʼ: **"Our Lord! Keep perfect our light for us and grant us forgiveness. Verily, You are Able to do all things."** Mujāhid, Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and others said this is the statement the believers will make on the Day of Resurrection *when they witness the light of the hypocrites being extinguished*. That is what gives the prayer its urgency: they are asking for their own light to be completed at the very moment they watch someone else's go out. Even there, they ask for forgiveness — not standing on their record, but on His power over all things.

The fear of disgrace on that Day is not only for ordinary believers. Imām Ahmad recorded that a man from the tribe of Banū Kinānah said: "I prayed behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during the year of the Conquest (of Makkah), and heard him say, *O Allah! Please, do not disgrace me on the Day of Resurrection.*" In the hour of his greatest worldly victory, entering Makkah, his prayer was about a different Day.

## Ayah 9: the struggle

"O Prophet! Strive hard against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be severe against them; their abode will be Hell, and worst indeed is that destination."

Ibn Kathīr explains that Allah the Exalted orders His Messenger ﷺ to perform jihad against both groups, but by two different means: the disbelievers with weapons and armaments, and the hypocrites by establishing Allah's legislated penal code.

"And be severe against them" — Ibn Kathīr: that is in this life. "Their abode will be Hell, and worst indeed is that destination" — that is in the Hereafter.

Note where the ayah leaves the passage. Ayah 6 said protect *your own* from the Fire; ayah 9 names those whose abode the Fire will be, with no softening. The same Fire the believer is told to shield his household from is the end of the road for those who set themselves against the message.

## Living it

The passage is unusually concrete, so the response can be too.

- **Start with yourself.** The command is *yourselves* before *your families*. Ibn ʿAbbās: work in the obedience of Allah, avoid disobedience of Allah.
- **Teach.** The Prophet's ﷺ answer to ʿUmar was instruction — tell them what Allah prohibited, tell them what Allah enjoined. Qatādah adds the part people skip: *help them act upon it.*
- **Begin early and stay with it.** Prayer ordered at seven, taken seriously by ten.
- **Repent as ʿAlī described it**, not just as a feeling: carry out the duties you missed, restore rights you usurped, seek the pardon of anyone you wronged, and resolve.
- **Do not bank on your deeds.** "Your actions alone cannot salvage you." Repent hard; hope in His grace.
- **Ask for the light.** The believers on that Day are still asking — "Our Lord! Keep perfect our light for us and grant us forgiveness." A prayer worth learning while there is still time for prayers to be accepted.

passages.title: Four women, two destinies
passages.tafsir:
Surah at-Tahrim closes with four portraits of women: two who lived inside the household of prophethood and were lost, and two who were saved — one of them married to the worst tyrant on earth, and one of them married to no one at all. The thread holding ayat 10–12 together is a single principle stated twice, once negatively and once positively: **nearness to a righteous person saves nobody, and nearness to a corrupt person ruins nobody.** Each soul stands on its own faith.

## Why these examples come here

The ayah just before this passage commands the Prophet ﷺ to strive hard against the disbelievers and the hypocrites and to be severe with them. Ibn Kathir explains it in two halves: the striving is against the disbelievers with weapons and armaments and against the hypocrites by establishing Allah's legislated penal code; "be severe against them" describes this life, and "their abode will be Hell" describes the next.

That raises a question for anyone whose daily life is shared with people who do not believe. Does all that closeness count for something?

Ibn Kathir gives the answer as the very meaning of ayah 10. He heads this section, "The Disbeliever shall never benefit from His Believing Relative on the Day of Resurrection," and explains that Allah sets forth this example for "the disbelievers who live together in this life with Muslims" — their mixing and mingling with Muslims will not help them, nor avail them with Allah, "until and unless they gain faith in their hearts." When the picture is flipped in ayah 11, he reads it as the mirror-image reassurance: this is a parable made for the believers, that if they need to, their association with the disbelievers will not harm them. He connects it to Allah's words in Surah Al 'Imran: "Let not the believers take the disbelievers as protecting friends instead of the believers, and whoever does that, will never be helped by Allah in any way, except you indeed fear a danger from them" (3:28).

So this is not a story collection. It is an argument, and the four women are its evidence.

## Ayah 10 — the two who had everything and lost it

"Allah sets forth an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Nuh and the wife of Lut. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they both betrayed them. So they availed them not against Allah, and it was said: 'Enter the Fire along with those who enter!'"

The Arabic says the two women "were under two servants from among Our righteous servants." Ibn Kathir unpacks what that meant: they were the wives of two of Allah's Messengers, "their companions by day and night, eating with them and sleeping with them, as much as any marriage contains of interaction between spouses." If proximity could save, these two were beyond argument — they lived in the same house as the men receiving revelation.

**"They both betrayed them" — betrayed in what?**

This is the point on which the ayah turns, and Ibn Kathir is emphatic. The word **khanatahuma** (they betrayed them) "does not pertain to committing illegal sexual intercourse, but to refusing to accept the religion." He explains that they did not adhere to the faith sent through their husbands nor accept their message. And he adds that the wives of the Prophets were immune from committing illegal sexual intercourse, on account of the honour Allah granted His Prophets — a point he says he had already established in Surah an-Nur.

He then brings the early authorities. Al-'Awfi reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "They betrayed them by not following their religion." And that report gives the concrete detail of what the treachery looked like day to day: the wife of Nuh (peace be upon him) used to expose his secrets, informing his oppressive people whenever any person embraced the faith with Nuh; and the wife of Lut (peace be upon him) used to inform the people of the city, who committed the awful act, whenever a guest was entertained by her husband. Ad-Dahhak reported that Ibn 'Abbas said: "No wife of a Prophet ever committed adultery and fornication. Rather, they betrayed them by refusing to follow their religion." Ibn Kathir notes that 'Ikrimah, Sa'id bin Jubayr, Ad-Dahhak and others said the same.

Sit with the shape of that treachery. Each woman used the one thing marriage gave her — inside knowledge — against the mission of the man who gave it to her. She knew who had believed; she knew who had arrived at the door. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point plainly: in matters of religion they opposed their husbands and secretly sided with the unbelievers and pagans, and their marital relation with the prophets could not save them from the punishment.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes that the name of Nuh's wife is said to be Waghilah and the name of Lut's wife Walihah, citing Qurtubi, and adds that some scholars have attributed other names to them — a healthy reminder of how lightly such details are held.

**"So they availed them not against Allah."** Ibn Kathir's reading is stark: all that intimate knowledge of their husbands neither helped them nor prevented punishment, because the wives were disbelievers. Then the verdict, addressed — as Ibn Kathir specifies — to these two wives: "Enter the Fire along with those who enter." *Along with those who enter.* No side door for the wife of a prophet. She walks in with the crowd.

## Ayah 11 — the believer inside the tyrant's house

Then the picture inverts. "And Allah has set forth an example for those who believe: the wife of Fir'awn, when she said: 'My Lord! Build for me a home with You in Paradise, and save me from Fir'awn and his work, and save me from the people who are wrongdoers.'"

Ibn Kathir names her: **Asiyah bint Muzahim**, may Allah be pleased with her.

Qatadah's comment is one of the most bracing lines in the whole tafsir: "Fir'awn was the most tyrannical among the people of the earth and the most disbelieving. By Allah! His wife was not affected by her husband's disbelief, because she obeyed her Lord. Therefore, let it be known that Allah is the Just Judge Who will not punish anyone except for their own sins."

**How she came to faith, and what it cost.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, places her belief at the point when Musa (peace be upon him) accomplished his task in defeating the sorcerers, who then embraced the Mosaic faith; she embraced it too. Fir'awn ordered that she be tortured severely and tormented harshly. According to some reports her hands and feet were pegged with nails to the ground and a huge rock was placed on her chest so that she could not move, and in that state she made the supplication in this ayah. According to other reports it was suggested that a huge rock be dropped on her, and they had hardly dropped it when she prayed the words quoted in the verse.

Ibn Kathir preserves two narrations Ibn Jarir recorded. Sulayman said: "The wife of Fir'awn was tortured under the sun, and when Fir'awn would finish the torture session, the angels would shade her with their wings. She was shown her house in Paradise." And Al-Qasim bin Abi Bazzah said: Fir'awn's wife used to ask, "Who prevailed?" When she was told, "Musa and Harun prevailed," she said, "I believe in the Lord of Musa and Harun." Fir'awn sent his aides to her with instructions to find the biggest stone: if she insists on keeping her faith, throw it on her, otherwise she is my wife. "When they came to her, she looked up to the sky and was able to see her house in Paradise. She persisted on the faith and her soul was then captured. The stone was thrown on her lifeless body."

Both commentaries carry the same ending: the answer arrived before the sentence was carried out. She saw the house. Her soul departed while she was looking at it. The rock fell on a body she had already left. Maʿārif draws out the weight of that — she was shown her place in Paradise **right here in this world**, and the infidelity of her husband did not prove to be an impediment to that rank.

**What she asked for.** She asks for a home — and the request names her Lord's nearness as part of it: "Build for me a home *with You* in Paradise," or in Maʿārif's rendering, "build for me, *near You*, a house in the Paradise."

Then two rescues. "Save me from Fir'awn **and his work**" — which Ibn Kathir explains as: deliver me from him, *because I am innocent of his actions*. She asks to be separated not only from the man but from what he did. And "save me from the people who are wrongdoers" — she does not stop at one man; she asks for deliverance from a wrongdoing people.

In the state those reports describe — pinned, immobilised, awaiting the stone — she could not alter her circumstances by an inch. So she asked Allah for the one exit no tyrant can seal.

## Ayah 12 — Maryam, who belonged to no one but Allah

The fourth example is unlike the other three: Maryam (peace be upon her) is not defined by a husband at all. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point directly — she was not the wife of anyone, yet her faith and virtuous deeds earned her so high a degree that she was invested with the perfections of the prophets, even though she was not a prophet according to the majority of scholars. A passage that began by measuring women against their husbands ends with a woman measured against nothing but her own faith and deeds.

Allah praises her in four strokes.

**"Who guarded her chastity."** Ibn Kathir: she protected and purified her honour, by being chaste and free of immorality. Set that against ayah 10. Two wives of prophets are declared *unfaithful* in a sense that, as Ibn Kathir insists, had nothing to do with the body; one unmarried woman is honoured for a chastity that stands alongside her faith. The Qur'an will not let the reader collapse the two categories.

**"And We breathed into it through Our Ruh."** Ibn Kathir explains **Ruhina** here as the angel Jibril: Allah sent Jibril to Maryam, and he came to her in the shape of a man in every respect; Allah commanded him to blow into a gap of her garment, and that breath went into her womb — this is how 'Isa (peace be upon him) was conceived.

**"And she testified to the truth of her Lord's Kalimat and His Kutub."** Here the two commentaries take complementary angles. Ibn Kathir reads **kalimat** (words) and **kutub** (books) as Allah's decree and His legislation — what He determines and what He commands. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads "the words of her Lord" as the scriptures revealed to the Prophets, and "the Books" as the well-known celestial Books: the Injil, the Zabur and the Torah. Between them you get the whole picture of a believing heart: it accepts what Allah *sends down*, and it accepts what Allah *decrees* — and in her case the decree was a test almost no one has been asked to carry.

**"And she was of the qanitin."** Maʿārif explains that this describes her quality: **qanitin** is the plural of **qanit**, and it signifies "devout and obedient." She is counted among the devout.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir brings two reports here.

Imam Ahmad recorded from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ drew four lines on the ground and asked, "Do you know what these lines represent?" They said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He ﷺ said: "The best among the women of Paradise are Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, Fatimah bint Muhammad, Maryam bint 'Imran and Asiyah bint Muzahim, wife of Fir'awn."

And it is confirmed in the Two Sahihs from Abu Musa Al-Ash'ari that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Many men have reached the level of perfection, but none among women have reached this level except Asiyah — Fir'awn's wife, Maryam — the daughter of 'Imran, and Khadijah — the daughter of Khuwaylid. And no doubt, the superiority of 'A'ishah to other women is like the superiority of Tharid to other meals."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes the report of Abu Musa as well — that whilst many men have attained spiritual perfection, among women only Asiyah, the wife of Fir'awn, and Maryam, the daughter of 'Imran, achieved it — citing it as "Bukhari and Muslim as quoted by Mazhari." Mazhari comments that "perfection" in this context apparently refers to the characteristics of prophethood, and that despite being a woman she achieved them.

Read that beside ayah 11 and the scale of the reversal lands. The woman whose husband was, in Qatadah's words, the most tyrannical and most disbelieving of the people of the earth is ranked by the Prophet ﷺ among the finest of all the women of Paradise. Allah preserved her as an example set for the believers.

## Living it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the practical conclusion with unusual bluntness, and it cuts both ways. Commenting on verse 11, it says the verse serves as a warning to the unbelievers who think that they will attain salvation merely by their companionship with believers: the good company will not rescue them in the Hereafter if they persist in their disbelief. And then the guarantee running the other way: so likewise, a disbeliever's disbelief will not harm a believing relative.

Hence its conclusion: the wives of the prophets and of the friends of Allah (*auliya'*, those close to Him through faith and obedience) should not carelessly take for granted that they will attain salvation on account of their husbands, nor should the wife of a disbeliever think that his disbelief will harm her. **Every person, man or woman, should be concerned about his or her own faith and action.**

Three things follow.

**Access is not faith.** You can live in the house where revelation is being received and still be on the other side of it — that is precisely what Ibn Kathir says these two wives proved. Sitting in the study circle, descending from scholars, marrying into a religious family, living among Muslims — Ibn Kathir's words are that mixing and mingling will not avail anyone with Allah "until and unless they gain faith in their hearts." Ask what you actually believe and actually obey, not who you are standing next to.

**Circumstances do not decide you.** Asiyah, in the state those reports describe, could not change a single detail of her situation. What she could do was believe, disown her husband's deeds, and ask her Lord for a home with Him — and Qatadah's verdict is that her husband's disbelief did not affect her, because she obeyed her Lord. Whatever your situation has fixed in place, it has not fixed your heart.

**Pray like her.** Her du'a is worth memorising as a pattern: ask for a home with your Lord, near Him; ask to be delivered from a wrongdoer *and from his deeds*, saying with her, "I am innocent of his actions"; ask to be saved from a wrongdoing people, not from one man only. She made that supplication in the worst circumstances a person could be in, and Allah showed her the answer before the sentence could be carried out.
